procedural_history.impugned_order: Judgment and order dated July 17, 1964 of the Patna High Court in Criminal Revision No. 597 of 1963, setting aside the acquittal of the appellant and directing his retrial.
procedural_history.high_court_proceedings: A private party filed a revision application in the Patna High Court against the acquittal of the appellant by the Sessions Judge. The High Court, in its revisional powers under s. 439 of the Code of Criminal Procedure, went into the evidence minutely, questioned the Sessions Judge's findings, and gave its own interpretation of the evidence de novo. The High Court then directed the retrial of the appellant.
procedural_history.supreme_court_posture: The appellant appealed to the Supreme Court by special leave, challenging the High Court's order for retrial. The Supreme Court considered whether the High Court, in exercising its revisional powers under s. 439 of the Code of Criminal Procedure, acted in accordance with the principles settled by the Supreme Court for interference with acquittal by way of revision filed by a private party.

directions: the order of retrial is therefore revoked

issue.issue_text: Whether a High Court, in exercising its revisional powers under Section 439 of the Code of Criminal Procedure, can set aside an acquittal and order a retrial by re-appraising the evidence and reaching conclusions contrary to the trial court.

facts: The appellant was acquitted by the Sessions Judge.
A private party filed a revision petition with the High Court against the acquittal.
Exercising its revisional powers under Section 439 of the Code of Criminal Procedure, the High Court set aside the acquittal and ordered a retrial.

In its judgment, the High Court minutely re-examined the evidence, questioned every finding of the Sessions Judge, and gave its own interpretation of the evidence, reaching conclusions contrary to the trial court.
law: A High Court can interfere with an acquittal in its revisional jurisdiction only in exceptional circumstances.
The grounds for interference include a "manifest illegality" in the judgment or a "gross miscarriage of justice."

Interference is also justified for a "glaring defect of procedure," such as the trial court lacking jurisdiction, shutting out admissible evidence, considering inadmissible evidence, or overlooking evidence.
A High Court is not entitled to interfere simply because the trial court took a wrong view of the law or misappreciated the evidence.
The revisional power is not the same as an appellate power; the High Court cannot re-weigh the evidence as if it were hearing an appeal against acquittal.
application: The Supreme Court found that the High Court had not identified any manifest illegality or glaring procedural defect in the Sessions Judge's decision that would justify ordering a retrial.
Instead, the High Court had acted as if it were an appellate court by re-weighing the evidence from its own point of view and substituting its own inferences for those of the Sessions Judge.
The Court noted that the High Court's approach was a breach of the established principles limiting its revisional powers in cases of acquittal.
reasoning.conclusion: The Supreme Court concluded that the High Court erred by exceeding its limited revisional jurisdiction. It should not have re-appraised the evidence merely to arrive at a different factual conclusion. Therefore, the Supreme Court rejected the High Court's reasoning, set aside its order for a retrial, and restored the original acquittal of the appellant.

arguments.issue_text: Whether a High Court, in exercising its revisional powers under Section 439 of the Code of Criminal Procedure, can set aside an acquittal and order a retrial by re-appraising the evidence and reaching conclusions contrary to the trial court.
appellant_arguments: The High Court erred by treating a revision application as if it were an appeal against acquittal, making no distinction between its appellate and revisional powers.
The High Court improperly went into the evidence minutely, questioned every finding of the Sessions Judge, and gave its own interpretation of the evidence de novo.
The Sessions Judge acted within his rights in appraising the evidence, finding it unsatisfactory and doubtful, and acquitting the accused.
Except for one minor error of law regarding cross-examination, the High Court found no defect of procedure or law in the Sessions Judge's judgment that would justify setting aside the acquittal.
The High Court should not have set aside the acquittal and ordered a retrial in a revision filed by a private party, especially when the Sessions Judge's view of the evidence was a plausible one.
respondent_arguments: The Sessions Judge's acquittal was based on a flawed and unsatisfactory appraisal of the evidence.
The Sessions Judge committed an error of law by remarking that defence witnesses ought to have been cross-examined with reference to their previous police statements.

The High Court was justified in exercising its revisional powers to correct a manifest injustice by re-examining the evidence and ordering a retrial, as the Sessions Judge's conclusions were incorrect.

cases.principle: It was cited for the principle outlining the grounds that entitle a High Court to set aside an acquittal in a revision and order a retrial.

cases.case_name: Logendranath Jha and others v. Shri Polailal Biswas
cases.principle: It was followed for the principles governing the High Court's exercise of revisional powers to interfere with an acquittal.

cases.case_name: K. Chinnaswamy Reddy v. State of Andhra Pradesh
cases.principle: It was followed for the principles governing the High Court's exercise of revisional powers to interfere with an acquittal.

ratio_decidendi.ratio: A High Court, exercising its revisional powers against an acquittal at the request of a private party, cannot interfere by re-weighing the evidence and reaching a contrary conclusion. Interference is only permissible if there is a manifest illegality, a gross miscarriage of justice, a glaring defect of procedure, an error on a point of law, or a complete failure to appraise the evidence.
obiter: By ordering a retrial, the dice is loaded against the accused, because however much the High Court may caution the Subordinate Court, it is always difficult to re-weigh the evidence ignoring the opinion of the High Court.

judicial_reasoning.core_finding: The High Court erred by treating the revision application as if it were an appeal against acquittal. The learned Judge re-weighed the evidence from his own point of view and reached inferences contrary to those of the Sessions Judge on almost every point. This is not the High Court's duty when dealing in revision with an acquittal, especially when the government has not chosen to file an appeal. In doing so, the High Court did not attend to the established rules and acted in breach of them, as none of the limited grounds for interfering with an acquittal in revision, such as a manifest illegality or a glaring procedural defect, were present in the case.
legal_tests_applied: To set aside an acquittal in a revision and order a retrial, there must exist a manifest illegality in the judgment of the Court of Session ordering the acquittal or there must be a gross miscarriage of justice.
The High Court is not entitled to interfere even if a wrong view of law is taken by the Court of Session or if there is misappreciation of evidence.

The High Court is entitled in revision to set aside an acquittal if there is an error on a point of law or no appraisal of the evidence at all; it is not sufficient to say that the judgment under revision is 'perverse' or 'lacking in true correct perspective'.

An interference in revision with an order of acquittal can only take place if there is a glaring defect of procedure such as that the Court had no jurisdiction to try the case, or the Court had shut out some material evidence which was admissible, or attempted to take into account evidence which was not admissible, or had overlooked some evidence.
policy_considerations: By ordering a retrial, the dice is loaded against the accused, because however much the High Court may caution the Subordinate Court, it is always difficult to re-weigh the evidence ignoring the opinion of the High Court.

The High Court's powers in a revision filed by a private party against an acquittal are more circumscribed than in an appeal filed by the State, and it should not take upon itself the duty of re-appraising evidence de novo in such a case.
